new_statements.relation_note: Lexical tone contrast exists but is not. grammatical tone (H/L pattern replacement, rising, falling) marks distal action, progressive, 2sg object and benefactive. No mention of stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Pongu has lexical tone (H vs L minimal pair bishúwá vs bishúwà, left unwritten in the orthography) and an extensive system of grammatical tone: distal ('action in a distant location') verb forms replace (L)LH with (H)HL; progressive is marked by a rising tone on the final syllable of the word before the verb; a 2sg object by a falling tone on that syllable; benefactive by a rising tone on the verb's penultimate syllable (replaced by vowel length in distal forms). Nothing is said about stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Iterative verb forms add a syllable so the benefactive rising-tone syllable is no longer penultimate (slide 19: kǔsa -> kǔsaga, kindǎ̱ga̱ -> kindǎ̱ga̱ga̱); in distal forms the benefactive rising tone is replaced by a long vowel (slide 20).

new_statements.quote: James Macdonell gave an overview of the Pongu [tərĩ́] language project based on fieldwork started in 2003, but beginning permanently in 2005. Pongu is spoken near Kagara in Niger State. Alphabet charts, a suggested orthography and preliminary literacy materials are all available for Pongu. As with many other languages, tone-marking is an issue in the orthography and the present decision is not to mark lexical tone and to try and find an acceptable system of marking grammatical tone. Some alternative orthographic options in this area were presented.

tone_statements.citation: MacDonell, James and Smith, Philip (2004). A phonological and grammatical sketch of the Pongu language.
tone_statements.quote: Pangu has both lexical and grammatical tone. ... There are two level tones, High and Low. ... Trisyllabic roots have been found to carry all eight possible combinations of High and Low tones. ... Pangu roots also exhibit Falling and Rising tones. No distribution pattern associating these contour tones with a particular syllable position has been established, though their association with long vowels is noted. So these tones are understood to be phonemic. ... The system of High, Low, Falling and Rising tones can be extended to the entire lexicon of the language.
tone_statements.locator: Part I, §7 Tone and §7.1 Lexical Tone Patterns, pp. 41-42
tone_statements.summary: H, L plus phonemic Falling/Rising tied to long vowels; all 8 H/L patterns on trisyllabic roots; floating L marks 2sg object (p.63); fn.82 p.107 reports 'automatic downstep' after a reduced L prefix.
